cse-2026-2-ga-1.approach: Find the common meaning of the three given words — all three mean *to make something happen faster* — and pick the option that shares it.
concepts: Word meaning from a common thread

steps.title: Common meaning of the given words
steps.body:
- **Expedite**: to make a process happen sooner or more quickly.
- **Hasten**: to make something happen sooner; to hurry.
- **Hurry**: to move or act quickly; to make something go faster.

The shared idea is **speeding something up**.

steps.title: Test each option against "speed up"
steps.body:
- **Accelerate**: to increase speed / make happen sooner — matches.
- **Retard**: to slow down — the *opposite*.
- **Provide**: to supply — unrelated to speed.
- **Disable**: to make unable to work — unrelated.

So the blank is **Accelerate** — option (A).

steps.title: Confirm by substitution
steps.body: "The manager asked the team to **accelerate** the delivery" means the same as *expedite / hasten / hurry* the delivery — the series Expedite, Hasten, Hurry, **Accelerate** is complete.

optionAnalysis.reason: Accelerate = increase speed, the same sense as expedite, hasten and hurry.
Retard means to slow down or delay — an antonym of the given words.
Provide means to supply something; it has nothing to do with speed.
Disable means to make something unable to function; unrelated to speed.

cse-2026-2-ga-1.shortcut: All three cue words are "make it faster"; only one option is a speed word that is not an antonym — Accelerate.
pitfalls: Picking the antonym (Retard) because it is also a "speed" word — the question asks for a similar meaning.
cse-2026-2-ga-1.verification: Substitute: "We must accelerate / expedite / hasten the process" — all read naturally with the same meaning.

cse-2026-2-ga-2.approach: Read Panel I on its $6 \times 6$ unit grid and list the **white (missing) cells** row by row. The missing part must fill exactly those cells as it stands in the square, so compare that cell pattern with each Panel II shape.
cse-2026-2-ga-2.given:
Panel I is a $6 \times 6$ square PQRS. Counting rows from the top (S–R side) and columns from the left (S–P side):

| Row | Black cells | White cells |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 1–6 | — |
| 2 | 1, 3, 4 | 2, 5, 6 |
| 3 | 1, 6 | 2, 3, 4, 5 |
| 4 | 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 | 4 |
| 5 | 1, 5, 6 | 2, 3, 4 |
| 6 | 1–6 | — |

steps.title: Count the cells of the missing part
steps.body: White cells per row: $3 + 4 + 1 + 3 = 11$. Black cells: $6 + 3 + 2 + 5 + 3 + 6 = 25$, and $25 + 11 = 36 = 6 \times 6$, so the grid reading is consistent. The other part has **11 unit squares**.

steps.title: Shape of the missing part
steps.body:
The white cells occupy rows 2–5 and columns 2–6, i.e. a $4 \times 5$ box. Shifting the columns so the box starts at column 1 gives:

| Row | Cells |
|---|---|
| top | 1, 4, 5 |
| 2nd | 1, 2, 3, 4 |
| 3rd | 3 |
| bottom | 1, 2, 3 |

In words: a post on the left and a two-cell arm on the top right, a 4-cell bar, a 1-cell stem under cell 3, and a **3-cell bottom bar starting under the left post**.

steps.title: Compare with the four shapes
steps.body:
All four shapes share the top row (1, 4, 5) and the 4-cell second row, so only the lower half decides:

- (i): stem 3, bottom bar 1–4 (**4 cells**, total 12) — too long.
- (ii): stem 3, bottom bar 2–4 — shifted one cell right.
- (iii): stem 3, bottom bar **1–3** — exact match, 11 cells.
- (iv): stem 3–4, bottom 2–3 — wrong shape.

The other part is **(iii)** — option (C).

scene.caption: Bottom bar of the gap = columns 2–4 (3 cells): only (iii) matches

optionAnalysis.reason: (i) has a 4-cell bottom bar (12 cells in all); the gap in Panel I has only 3 white cells in that row (columns 2–4).
(ii) has the right cell count, but its bottom bar is shifted one cell right, so it would overlap the black cell at column 5 of row 5.
(iii) fills exactly the 11 white cells: top 1, 4, 5; then 1–4; then 3; then 1–3.
(iv) has a 2-cell-wide third row and a 2-cell bottom bar; Panel I has one white cell (column 4) in row 4 and three in row 5.

cse-2026-2-ga-2.shortcut: Only the bottom bar differs in a useful way: Panel I's lowest white strip is 3 cells long and starts directly under the left white post — only (iii) has that.
pitfalls: Counting only the outline and missing that (i) and (iii) differ by a single cell in the bottom bar.
Rotating or flipping the shapes — the missing part must fit as drawn.
cse-2026-2-ga-2.verification: Place (iii) back into the square: its 11 cells cover rows 2–5 exactly where Panel I is white, and $25 + 11 = 36$ fills PQRS completely with no overlap.

cse-2026-2-ga-3.approach: Four independent days with $P(\text{cloudy}) = \tfrac12$ is a binomial experiment. Count the arrangements with exactly three cloudy days and multiply by the probability of one arrangement.

steps.title: Probability of one particular arrangement
steps.body:
For a fixed pattern such as C C C S, independence gives
$$P = \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 \times \tfrac12 = \tfrac{1}{16}.$$
Because $P(\text{cloudy}) = P(\text{sunny}) = \tfrac12$, **every** one of the $2^4 = 16$ patterns has probability $\tfrac{1}{16}$.

steps.title: Count patterns with exactly one sunny day
steps.body: Choose which of the 4 days is sunny: $\binom{4}{3} = \binom{4}{1} = 4$ patterns (SCCC, CSCC, CCSC, CCCS).

steps.title: Multiply
steps.body:
$$P(3\text{ cloudy}, 1\text{ sunny}) = \binom{4}{3}\left(\tfrac12\right)^3\left(\tfrac12\right)^1 = 4 \times \tfrac{1}{16} = \tfrac{4}{16} = \tfrac14.$$
Answer: $\tfrac14$ — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: $3/4$ is far too large — it would leave only $1/4$ for all the other 12 patterns, which hold $12/16$.
$2/3$ has no basis in a count over $2^4 = 16$ equally likely outcomes.
$3/8 = 6/16$ is the probability of exactly **two** cloudy days ($\binom42 = 6$), not three.

pitfalls: Forgetting the factor $\binom43 = 4$ for the position of the sunny day (gives $1/16$, not offered).
Using $\binom42 = 6$ by mistake, which gives $3/8$.
cse-2026-2-ga-3.verification: The five binomial probabilities $1, 4, 6, 4, 1$ over 16 sum to $16/16 = 1$; the "3 cloudy" bar is $4/16$.

cse-2026-2-ga-4.approach: Convert money invested into the **number of shares** bought, value those shares at the next day's prices, and compare the total selling value with the total investment.
cse-2026-2-ga-4.given:
| Stock | Buy price | Amount invested | Sell price |
|---|---|---|---|
| A | Rs. 50 | Rs. 100 | Rs. 55 |
| B | Rs. 80 | Rs. 80 | Rs. 70 |

steps.title: Shares bought
steps.body:
Stock A: $\dfrac{100}{50} = 2$ shares. Stock B: $\dfrac{80}{80} = 1$ share.
Total invested $= 100 + 80 = \text{Rs. }180$.

steps.title: Value at the selling prices
steps.body:
Stock A: $2 \times 55 = 110$. Stock B: $1 \times 70 = 70$.
Total received $= 110 + 70 = \text{Rs. }180$.

steps.title: Profit
steps.body: $\text{Profit} = 180 - 180 = \text{Rs. }0$ — the gain on A ($+10$) exactly cancels the loss on B ($-10$). Option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: Gain on A $= 2 \times (55-50) = +10$; loss on B $= 1 \times (80-70) = -10$; net $0$.
Rs. 5 is the gain on a **single** share of A, forgetting that two shares were bought and ignoring B's loss.
Rs. 10 is only the gain on A; it ignores the Rs. 10 loss on B.
Rs. 20 adds the two changes instead of netting them (or treats B's fall as a gain).

pitfalls: Using the price change per share without multiplying by the number of shares.
Ignoring the loss on Stock B.
cse-2026-2-ga-4.verification: Percent check: A rises $10\%$ on Rs. 100 ($+10$), B falls $12.5\%$ on Rs. 80 ($-10$); net $0$.

cse-2026-2-ga-5.approach: Write the sentence as an implication $R \rightarrow D$ (raining → peacocks dance). An implication is logically equivalent only to its **contrapositive** $\neg D \rightarrow \neg R$; its converse and inverse do not follow.
cse-2026-2-ga-5.given: $R$: it is raining. $D$: peacocks dance. Given: $R \rightarrow D$.

steps.title: Translate each option
steps.body:
- (A) "Peacocks dance **only when** it is raining": $D ightarrow R$ (converse).
- (B) "When peacocks dance, it is raining": $D ightarrow R$ (converse).
- (C) "When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining": $
eg D ightarrow 
eg R$ (contrapositive).
- (D) "When it is not raining, peacocks do not dance": $
eg R ightarrow 
eg D$ (inverse).

steps.title: Which form must be true?
steps.body:
$R ightarrow D \equiv 
eg R \lor D \equiv D \lor 
eg R \equiv 
eg D ightarrow 
eg R$. So the contrapositive (C) is **necessarily** true: if peacocks are not dancing, it cannot be raining (else they would dance).

The converse and inverse can fail: peacocks may also dance on a sunny day — the sentence says nothing about that case.

steps.title: Counter-example for the other options
steps.body:
Take a dry, sunny day on which peacocks dance. The given sentence is not violated (it only speaks about rainy days), yet
- (A) and (B) claim dancing implies rain — false here;
- (D) claims no rain implies no dancing — false here.
No such world can break (C): if it rained, the peacocks would dance. Hence only (C) is **necessarily** true.

answer.value: **When peacocks are not dancing, it is not raining** — option (C)

optionAnalysis.reason: "Dance only when raining" is $D \rightarrow R$ — the converse; peacocks dancing on a dry day does not contradict the given sentence.
"When peacocks dance, it is raining" is again the converse $D \rightarrow R$, not implied.
Contrapositive $\neg D \rightarrow \neg R$, logically equivalent to $R \rightarrow D$.
"Not raining → not dancing" is the inverse $\neg R \rightarrow \neg D$; it is equivalent to the converse, so it does not follow either.

cse-2026-2-ga-5.shortcut: Flip **and** negate: "raining → dance" becomes "not dance → not raining". Any option that only flips or only negates is wrong.
pitfalls: Reading "A only when B" as $B \rightarrow A$; it means $A \rightarrow B$.
Assuming the sentence also covers what happens when it is not raining.
cse-2026-2-ga-5.verification: Counter-example world: sunny day, peacocks dancing. The given sentence holds (no rain), yet (A), (B) and (D) all fail; (C) still holds.

cse-2026-2-ga-6.approach: State the relation in the first pair as a sentence — *water relieves thirst* — and apply the same relation to food.

steps.title: Form the bridge sentence
steps.body: Water is what we take to relieve **thirst**; the need water satisfies is thirst. So $P$ = Thirst.

steps.title: Apply it to food
steps.body:
Food is what we take to relieve **hunger**. So $Q$ = Hunger.

Water : Thirst :: Food : Hunger — option (A).

steps.title: Reject the other pairs
steps.body: In (B) $P$ = Drink is an *action* while $Q$ = Hunger is a *need*; in (C) $P$ = Thirst is a need while $Q$ = Satiated is the *state after* eating; in (D) Wet is a property of water and Critic has no link to food. Only (A) keeps the same relation on both sides.

optionAnalysis.reason: Same relation on both sides: substance → the need it satisfies (thirst, hunger).
"Drink" is an action done with water, while "Hunger" is a need — the two sides use different relations.
"Satiated" is the state after eating, not the need food relieves; it does not mirror "thirst".
"Wet" is a property of water and "Critic" is unrelated to food.

cse-2026-2-ga-6.shortcut: Pick the option where $P$ and $Q$ are the same kind of word: Thirst and Hunger are both needs.
pitfalls: Choosing a pair where only one half fits the relation (B or C).
cse-2026-2-ga-6.verification: Read it back: "Water quenches thirst as food satisfies hunger" — both halves use the same verb idea.

cse-2026-2-ga-7.approach: Count the filled dots in every tile. The counts $8, 1, 6 / 3, 5, ? / 4, 9, ?$ are the classic $3 \times 3$ **magic square** (every row, column and diagonal sums to 15), so the missing counts follow at once; the dot layout fixes which tile pattern to use.

steps.title: Count the filled dots
steps.body:
Row 1: $8, 1, 6$. Row 2: $3, 5, ?$. Row 3: $4, 9, ?$.
Row 1 sums to $8 + 1 + 6 = 15$, and the first column to $8 + 3 + 4 = 15$, the middle column to $1 + 5 + 9 = 15$ — the tiles form a magic square with sum 15.

steps.title: Check the dot layout
steps.body:
The tiles fill dots in a fixed order: up the right column first (1 = bottom-right, 2 = lower two of the right column, 3 = whole right column), then up the middle column (4, 5, 6), then up the left column (7 = add bottom-left, 8 = add middle-left, 9 = all).
So the missing top tile is 7 = right two columns + bottom-left, and the bottom tile is 2 = lower two dots of the right column. That is pair **(i)** — option (A).

optionAnalysis.reason: Top tile 7, bottom tile 2, both in the correct fill pattern; completes the magic square.
Top tile has 6 dots: row 2 would sum to $3 + 5 + 6 = 14 \ne 15$.
Bottom tile has 3 dots: row 3 would sum to $4 + 9 + 3 = 16 \ne 15$.
6 over 4: rows 2 and 3 would sum to 14 and 17.

cse-2026-2-ga-7.shortcut: 8-1-6 / 3-5-? / 4-9-? is the Lo Shu magic square: the missing numbers are 7 and 2 — only (i) shows 7 above 2.
pitfalls: Matching only one of the two tiles: (iii) has the right top tile, (ii) the right bottom tile.

cse-2026-2-ga-8.approach: The trip is a **Hamiltonian cycle**. For the grid (i), exhibit one. For (ii), use the degree-2 rule: a city with only two highways must use both of them in the cycle — and in (ii) that forces three cycle edges at one city, which is impossible.
cse-2026-2-ga-8.given: Figure (ii) labelled A (top-left), B (top-right), C (inner), D (left), E (bottom). Highways: A–B, A–C, A–D, C–E, D–E, B–E.

steps.title: Figure (i): build a tour on the 4 × 4 grid
steps.body:
Label rows 1–4 (top to bottom) and columns 1–4. Go along the top row $(1,1) \to (1,4)$, then snake back through columns 4, 3, 2 in rows 2–4: $(1,4) \to (2,4) \to (2,2)$ along row 2, down to $(3,2) \to (3,4)$, down to $(4,4) \to (4,1)$, then up column 1: $(4,1) \to (3,1) \to (2,1) \to (1,1)$.
It visits all $16$ cities once and returns to the start, so **(i) is possible**.

steps.title: Figure (ii): cities of degree 2 force their edges
steps.body: B has only highways A–B, B–E; C has only A–C, C–E; D has only A–D, D–E. Each of them must enter and leave on its only two highways, so the cycle must contain **all six** highways.

steps.title: Contradiction at A (and E)
steps.body:
Then A would lie on three cycle edges (A–B, A–C, A–D), but in a cycle every city has exactly 2. (A 5-city cycle also has only 5 edges, not 6.) So **no such trip exists for (ii)**.

Trip possible for (i) but not for (ii) — option (A).

scene.caption: A would need 3 cycle edges — impossible

optionAnalysis.reason: The 4×4 grid has a Hamiltonian cycle (the snake tour); in (ii) the three degree-2 cities force A onto three cycle edges.
Reversed: (i) does have a tour, and (ii) does not.
(ii) has no tour: B, C, D force all six highways into the cycle, giving A degree 3.
(i) does have a tour — an explicit one is shown in step 1.

cse-2026-2-ga-8.shortcut: Three degree-2 cities B, C, D all hang on A: a cycle can use at most 2 edges at A, so (ii) fails. A grid with an even number of rows always has a Hamiltonian cycle.
pitfalls: Confusing this trip (every city once — Hamiltonian) with using every highway once (Eulerian).
Trying random routes on (ii) instead of using the forced-edge argument.
cse-2026-2-ga-8.verification: Edge count for (ii): a cycle through 5 cities has exactly 5 edges, but the degree-2 cities force 6 edges into it — impossible. For (i), the chessboard colouring has 8 black and 8 white cities, as an alternating 16-city cycle requires, and the explicit tour above uses only grid highways.

cse-2026-2-ga-9.approach: Count the shaded cells in every row and column of each option and compare with the targets — rows $3, 1, 2, 2$ (top to bottom) and columns $2, 2, 2, 2$. Rows eliminate three options immediately.

steps.title: Column totals of (ii)
steps.body:
Columns of (ii): col 1 = rows 1, 4 → 2; col 2 = rows 2, 4 → 2; col 3 = rows 1, 3 → 2; col 4 = rows 1, 3 → 2. All equal 2 ✓.
So **(ii)** is shaded correctly — option (B).

steps.title: Cross-check the total
steps.body: Row targets sum to $3 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 8$ and column targets to $2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8$, so a valid grid has exactly 8 shaded cells. (ii) has $3 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 8$ ✓ and passes all eight line checks.

optionAnalysis.reason: (i) has 2 shaded cells in row 2 (needs 1) and 1 in row 3 (needs 2), though its columns are fine.
(ii) matches every row (3, 1, 2, 2) and every column (2, 2, 2, 2).
(iii) has 2 cells in row 2 and 1 in row 3; column 3 also has 3 shaded cells.
(iv) has 1 cell in row 3 and 3 in row 4.

cse-2026-2-ga-9.shortcut: Check row 3 (needs 2): only (ii) has two shaded cells there.
pitfalls: Checking columns only — option (i) passes every column test but fails the rows.

cse-2026-2-ga-10.approach: There are $6 \times 6 = 36$ equally likely ordered outcomes. List the prime sums possible (2, 3, 5, 7, 11) and count the ordered pairs giving each.

steps.title: Sample space and possible primes
steps.body: Ordered outcomes $(a, b)$: $6 \times 6 = 36$, all equally likely. Sums range from 2 to 12; the primes among them are $2, 3, 5, 7, 11$.

steps.title: Probability
steps.body: $$P = \frac{15}{36}\;\left(= \tfrac{5}{12}\right) \text{ — option (C).}$$

optionAnalysis.reason: $3/36$ counts only the sums 2 and 3 ($1 + 2$ outcomes) and misses 5, 7 and 11.
$13/36$ omits the two outcomes for sum 11 (or similar under-counting).
$1 + 2 + 4 + 6 + 2 = 15$ ordered outcomes out of 36.
$19/36$ over-counts — e.g. treating 9 as prime (adds 4).

cse-2026-2-ga-10.shortcut: Number of ways to roll sum $s$ is $6 - \lvert s - 7 \rvert$: for $s = 2, 3, 5, 7, 11$ that is $1, 2, 4, 6, 2$ → 15.
pitfalls: Counting unordered pairs, e.g. (1,2) and (2,1) once.
Forgetting 2 or 11, or treating 9 as prime.
cse-2026-2-ga-10.verification: The 6 × 6 sum table has exactly 15 cells with a prime sum (highlighted in the animation).

cse-2026-2-cs-1.approach: Name the special person $y$. "There is a person" gives $\exists y$ outermost; "everyone else" gives $\forall x$ with $x \ne y$. For each such $x$: $x$ knows $y$ and $y$ does not know $x$.

steps.title: Translate the inner condition
steps.body:
For a fixed other person $x 
e y$:
- "that person is known by everyone else" → $M(x, y)$ ($x$ knows $y$);
- "does not know anyone else" → $
eg M(y, x)$.
Combined: $(x 
e y) ightarrow (M(x,y) \land 
eg M(y,x))$. The implication restricts the claim to people other than $y$ — the right form for a universal.

steps.title: Attach the quantifiers
steps.body: One fixed person works against **all** others: $(\exists y)(\forall x)\,((x \ne y) \rightarrow (M(x,y) \land \neg M(y,x)))$ — option (A). The order $\exists y\,\forall x$ matters: the same $y$ must work for every $x$.

steps.title: Why the other prefixes fail
steps.body:
- $\forall y\,\exists x$: each person has *some* other person — no single special person.
- $\exists y\,\exists x$: choosing $x = y$ makes the implication vacuously true, so the formula says nothing.
- $\forall y\,\forall x$: demands that everyone is known by and knows no one else — contradictory as soon as there are two people.
Only $\exists y\,\forall x$ (option A) fits.

optionAnalysis.reason: One person $y$; every other $x$ knows $y$ and is not known by $y$ — exactly the statement.
$\forall y\,\exists x$ says every person has *someone* who knows them and whom they do not know — no single special person.
$\exists y\,\exists x$ with an implication is trivially true (pick $x = y$, making the antecedent false); it says nothing about everyone.
$\forall y\,\forall x$ demands this of **every** person, which is self-contradictory for two people ($M(x,y)$ and $\neg M(x,y)$).

cse-2026-2-cs-1.shortcut: "There is a person … everyone else" → $\exists y\,\forall x$; only one option has that prefix.
pitfalls: Swapping the quantifier order ($\forall\exists$ vs $\exists\forall$).
Mixing the argument order of $M$: "$y$ is known by $x$" is $M(x, y)$.
cse-2026-2-cs-1.verification: Model: people $\{p, q, r\}$ with $q$ and $r$ knowing $p$ and $p$ knowing nobody. (A) is true with $y = p$; (D) fails at $y = q$, since $p$ does not know $q$.

cse-2026-2-cs-2.approach: Each traversal is named after **when the node is visited** relative to its subtrees: in-order (between), pre-order (before), post-order (after). Left is always visited before right.

steps.title: Inorder
steps.body: In-order visits the node **in between** its subtrees: left subtree, node, right subtree → **L**.

steps.title: Preorder and postorder
steps.body:
Pre-order visits the node **before** both subtrees: node, left, right → **M**.
Post-order visits it **after** both: left, right, node → **N**.

steps.title: Pick the option
steps.body: I – L, II – M, III – N — option (A).

answer.value: **I – L, II – M, III – N** — option (A)

optionAnalysis.reason: Inorder = L-node-R, preorder = node-L-R, postorder = L-R-node.
Swaps inorder and preorder.
Swaps inorder and postorder.
Swaps preorder and postorder.

cse-2026-2-cs-2.shortcut: Pre = node first, Post = node last, In = node in the middle.
pitfalls: Mixing up preorder and postorder.
cse-2026-2-cs-2.verification: Tree with root 2, left child 1, right child 3: inorder 1 2 3 (L), preorder 2 1 3 (M), postorder 1 3 2 (N).

cse-2026-2-cs-3.approach: Use the definition: $M$ **decides** $L$ when $M$ halts on every input, accepting exactly the strings of $L$ and rejecting all others. Since "rejects" means halting in the reject state, "accepts every $w \in L$ and rejects every $w \notin L$" says the same thing.

steps.title: What "decides" requires
steps.body:
On every input $w \in \{0,1\}^*$ the machine must halt, and
- $w \in L \Rightarrow M$ accepts;
- $w \notin L \Rightarrow M$ rejects (halts in the reject state).
Both halves are needed; the halting requirement is implied by them, because accepting and rejecting are both halting outcomes.

steps.title: Options that state only part of it
steps.body:
- (A) Halting on all inputs alone does not say *which* strings are accepted — $M$ might decide a different language.
- (B) Accepting all of $L$ still allows $M$ to accept or loop on strings outside $L$ (it only gives $L \subseteq L(M)$).
- (C) Rejecting all of $\{0,1\}^* - L$ still allows $M$ to reject or loop on strings in $L$.

steps.title: The equivalent statement
steps.body: (D) Accepting every $w \in L$ and rejecting every $w \notin L$ means $M$ halts on every input (accept and reject are both halting states) with the correct verdict — exactly the definition of "$M$ decides $L$". Option (D).

answer.value: **$M$ accepts all strings in $L$ and rejects all strings in $\{0,1\}^* - L$** — option (D)

optionAnalysis.reason: Halting on all inputs is necessary but not sufficient: a machine that rejects everything halts on all inputs yet does not decide a non-empty $L$.
Only half the definition: strings outside $L$ could be accepted or cause looping (a recogniser need not even do that).
Only the other half: strings in $L$ could be rejected or loop.
Accept on $L$ + reject on the complement = halts on every input with the correct answer — the definition of deciding.

cse-2026-2-cs-3.shortcut: Decider = total + correct. Only (D) pins down the verdict on every string; totality then follows automatically.
pitfalls: Treating "halts on all inputs" as the definition of a decider — it must also give the right answer.
Confusing "decides" with "recognises" (accepts exactly $L$, may loop outside).
cse-2026-2-cs-3.verification: Counter-example to (A): $L = \{0\}$ and $M$ rejecting every input — $M$ halts everywhere but rejects $0 \in L$, so it does not decide $L$, while (D) correctly fails for this $M$.
